notes.title: Start here: BorrowBox and validate-before-mutate
notes.body:
BorrowBox is a small .NET equipment-lending demo: staff reserve, check out and return items. The course in `astraupskill/` follows one repair across four workflows: **validate before you mutate**. Build and check the new object (a `Reservation` or `Loan`) first, and only then change the live equipment record.

Suggested reading order (the course README asks for chapters in order):

1. `astraupskill/README.md`: the summary of the repair and the reading route.
2. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: Core (the rules), Infrastructure (the stores), API.
3. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: state machines, captured time, live references, and the table translating each idea to a real database.
4. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`, then `04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING.md`.
5. `05-PRACTICE.md`; try the exercises before opening `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`.

Half the quizzes in this pack ask "where in the code is this rule?", so keep `Loan.cs`, `Reservation.cs` and the two equipment stores open. The other half ask "which test check would really prove this goal?"; for those, chapter 04 is the key reading.

excerpts.quote: The selected improvement is validate-before-mutate in reservation, checkout, return, and expiry workflows.
Read the chapters in order. Chapter 01 maps the Core, Infrastructure, and API layers.

notes.title: Live references: why the in-memory store changes what a test proves
notes.body:
By default BorrowBox keeps its data in in-memory stores built on `ConcurrentDictionary`. The codebase map points out an important detail: these stores keep the **same object** you gave them, and `GetAsync` hands back that same live object, not a copy.

That idea, a *live reference*, matters for two kinds of question in this pack:

- **What has really changed?** If code changes an `EquipmentItem` it got from the store and then throws, ask what the store now contains. Work it out from how the store keeps its objects.
- **What does a check observe?** For any assertion in a test, ask where the value it reads comes from: a variable in the test, an object shared with the store, or a fresh read from storage.

A database store behaves differently from an in-memory one, and the concepts chapter has a table translating each in-memory idea into its database version. Read that table, and for each in-memory idea note what a database version would need to do instead.

excerpts.quote: Infrastructure stores are `ConcurrentDictionary` wrappers that retain entity references. `AddAsync` and `SaveAsync` store the same object, not a clone. That is useful for demonstrating side effects but does not provide multi-record durability. The SQLite adapter is available only for equipment; the teaching default does not select it. Tests live in Core, Infrastructure, and API projects. The focused lifecycle tests belong in `tests/BorrowBox.Infrastructure.Tests`, where all three in-memory stores can be composed.
## Candidate objects versus live aggregates

notes.title: Time and boundary equality: before, equal, after
notes.body:
Many bugs live at a boundary: what happens when two times are exactly equal? BorrowBox makes a deliberate choice for each rule, and the concepts chapter has a section, "Boundary equality, case by case". For each rule (reservation creation, expiry processing, loan due dates, return times) note what kind of value is compared, an exact instant or something else, and what happens on exact equality.

To test such rules you need "one minute before", "exactly equal" and "one minute after" to be exact values. Look at how the code obtains the current time, what the production setup registers for it, and what that design lets a test do differently.

When you read the code, find each time comparison (`<`, `<=`, `>`) and say out loud which side of the boundary it allows.

notes.title: Where BorrowBox already uses a conditional UPDATE
notes.body:
The finding: on a real database you do not take a C# `lock`. Instead you send one UPDATE that only matches the row if it is still Available, and you look at how many rows changed. 1 means you won the race; 0 means someone else did.

The key, `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:38-46`, is `TryCheckOutAsync` in the SQLite store. It uses `ExecuteUpdateAsync` with `row.Status == Available` in the `Where`, and returns the item only when `changed == 1`. The concepts chapter names these exact lines.

Why the other locations are wrong:
- `InMemoryEquipmentStore.cs:41-46`: this is the in-memory version, the C# `lock` the finding says gets replaced.
- `Loan.cs:74-80`: this is `CheckOutAsync` in the checkout service. It builds the `Loan` and *calls* `TryCheckOutAsync`; it does not run any UPDATE itself.

excerpts.quote: .Where(row => row.Id == id && row.Status == nameof(EquipmentStatus.Available)) .ExecuteUpdateAsync(
return changed == 1 ? await GetAsync(id, cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false) : null;
`changed == 1` means you won; `changed == 0` means somebody else did

notes.title: Proving a rejected reservation damages nothing
notes.body:
The goal has two halves: the call must be refused, **and** nothing must change. So the check needs three parts: the domain exception is thrown, the equipment is still Available, and the reservation store is empty. That is exactly Exercise 1 in the practice chapter.

Why it works: in the repaired `ReserveAsync`, `new Reservation(...)` runs before `equipment.Reserve()`. An expiry at 09:00 against a 10:00 clock fails in the constructor, so the equipment is never touched and nothing is added.

Why the other checks fall short:
- "The call succeeds and the worker releases it later": an expiry in the past must be refused, not accepted.
- "Only `Assert.ThrowsAsync`": the practice chapter says a test that names only the exception cannot catch a mutation leak. If `Reserve()` ran first, the exception would still be thrown.
- "Status Expired and equipment Reserved": the call throws, so no reservation comes back at all.

excerpts.quote: Inject a clock at 10:00 and call `ReserveAsync` with expiry 09:00. Assert the domain exception, Available equipment, and zero reservations.
A test that names only the exception cannot catch a mutation leak.
var reservation = new Reservation(Guid.NewGuid(), equipment.Id, borrower.Id, (clock ?? new SystemClock()).UtcNow, expiresAt); equipment.Reserve();

notes.title: What a database transaction would and would not fix
notes.body:
The goal asks for the course's verdict, which is in Solution 10, point 3. A transaction makes a group of database writes all-or-nothing. That fixes the "storage half" of a problem: the equipment row and the reservation row would roll back together. So the reservation/checkout **ordering** defect is a storage-atomicity problem.

The other three repairs are about decisions, not storage:
- `returnedAt < CheckedOutAt` is a domain rule; no isolation level rejects a nonsense time.
- "equipment must still be CheckedOut" is a precondition; a transaction makes a wrong write atomic, not correct.
- the expiry status check stops a write that is valid on its own; a transaction commits it.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- "All four, including C# objects": the chapter says EF Core rolls back the database, not your objects.
- "None, SQLite has no transactions": the chapter shows wrapping `ReserveAsync` in `BeginTransactionAsync`.
- "Only the return-time rule": that is the one rule the chapter says no isolation level enforces.

excerpts.quote: It does nothing about three of the four repairs in this course:
No isolation level rejects a nonsensical timestamp.
because EF Core rolls back the database, not your C# objects.

notes.title: Where an expiry equal to the reservation time is refused
notes.body:
The finding: an expiry exactly equal to the reservation instant must be refused with `reservation.expiry_invalid`. So the line we want uses `<=`, not `<`.

The key, `Reservation.cs:15`, is in the `Reservation` constructor: `if (expiresAt <= reservedAt) throw ... "reservation.expiry_invalid"`. Because of `<=`, equal times throw. The concepts chapter explains why: an item that is already due should never become Active.

What the other lines actually are:
- `InMemoryEquipmentStore.cs:43`: the "is the item Available?" check inside the checkout lock.
- `Loan.cs:13`: the loan due-date check, which compares calendar dates and allows equality.
- `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:41`: the `Where` clause of the conditional checkout UPDATE.

excerpts.quote: if (expiresAt <= reservedAt) throw new BorrowBoxException("reservation.expiry_invalid", "Expiry must be after reservation time.");
Equality fails because `Reservation`'s constructor tests `expiresAt <= reservedAt` (`Reservation.cs:15`), not `<`.

notes.title: Where the in-memory checkout lock lives
notes.body:
The finding: in the teaching setup (in-memory stores), two checkouts of the same item must give exactly one winner. That needs a lock around "is it Available? then check it out".

The key, `InMemoryEquipmentStore.cs:41`, is `lock (item)` inside `TryCheckOutAsync`. Inside the lock, it returns null unless the status is Available, then calls `item.CheckOut()`. The lock is per item, so two requests for the same item take turns, and the second one sees CheckedOut and loses.

What the other lines actually are:
- `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:30`: the start of `SaveAsync` in the SQLite store, loading a row to update. The SQLite store is not used in the teaching configuration.
- `Loan.cs:76`: `new Loan(...)` in the checkout service; it builds the candidate loan, it does not lock anything.
- `Reservation.cs:77`: `equipment.Reserve()` in the reservation workflow, a different operation.

excerpts.quote: lock (item) { if (item.Status != EquipmentStatus.Available) return Task.FromResult
`InMemoryEquipmentStore.TryCheckOutAsync` locks the item and changes it only if Available.

notes.title: Which guard keeps a return from going before checkout
notes.body:
The finding: one guard keeps `ReturnedAt` unset when someone tries to return a loan at a time before it was checked out. Remove it, and the return-before-checkout test fails because `ReturnedAt` gets a value.

The key, `Loan.cs:33`, is inside `Loan.Return`: `if (returnedAt < CheckedOutAt) throw ... "loan.return_time_invalid"`. The very next line sets `ReturnedAt`. So without the guard, the bad time would be stored. The solutions chapter lists this exact mutation exercise.

What the other lines actually are:
- `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:45`: the `changed == 1` result of the conditional checkout UPDATE; nothing to do with returns.
- `Reservation.cs:15`: the reservation expiry check, a different entity and a different rule.

excerpts.quote: if (returnedAt < CheckedOutAt) throw new BorrowBoxException("loan.return_time_invalid", "Return time cannot be before checkout."); ReturnedAt = returnedAt.ToUniversalTime();
Remove the `returnedAt < CheckedOutAt` guard and the return-before-checkout test should fail because `ReturnedAt` becomes non-null.

notes.title: Where the due date is compared to the UTC checkout date
notes.body:
The finding: the loan due date is a calendar date (`DateOnly`), and it is compared with the **UTC** date of checkout. At 23:45 UTC a same-day due date is fine; fifteen minutes later the UTC date has moved on, and the same due date would be "before checkout".

The key, `Loan.cs:13`, is in the `Loan` constructor: `if (dueOn < DateOnly.FromDateTime(checkedOutAt.UtcDateTime))`. `.UtcDateTime` is what makes it the UTC day, and `<` is why the same day is allowed.

What the other lines actually are:
- `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:45`: the conditional checkout result, `changed == 1`.
- `Reservation.cs:15`: the reservation expiry check; it compares two instants, not dates.

excerpts.quote: if (dueOn < DateOnly.FromDateTime(checkedOutAt.UtcDateTime)) throw new BorrowBoxException("loan.due_date_invalid", "Due date cannot be before checkout.");
so a same-day due date is legal even fifteen minutes before midnight UTC — and would be *illegal* fifteen minutes later.

notes.title: Where the expiry run picks due reservations
notes.body:
The finding: a reservation whose deadline is exactly `now` counts as due. So the selection must use `<=`.

The key, `Reservation.cs:121`, is inside `ReservationExpiryService.ExpireDueAsync`: the `Where` keeps items with `Status == Active && ExpiresAt <= now`. Note the contrast with the constructor on line 15, which forbids equality when *creating* a reservation. The concepts chapter says these two rules are separate on purpose.

What the other lines actually are:
- `InMemoryEquipmentStore.cs:43`: the Available check inside the in-memory checkout lock.
- `SqliteEquipmentStore.cs:41`: the `Where` of the SQLite conditional checkout UPDATE.
- `Loan.cs:13`: the loan due-date check against the UTC checkout date.

excerpts.quote: item.Status == ReservationStatus.Active && item.ExpiresAt <= now))
Expiry processing uses an inclusive comparison because a reservation whose deadline is exactly now is due.

notes.title: What the two-competing-checkouts test really proves
notes.body:
The goal is to state exactly what this test proves, no more. The test uses a "racing" fake store that makes two readers arrive together, then lets one `TryCheckOutAsync` win. It asserts that exactly one attempt succeeded. Because both are forced into the race and exactly one success is required, the test proves the per-item checkout is guarded.

Why the other statements fall short:
- "A failed checkout rolls back loan and equipment together": the stores have no rollback, and the test does not look at rollback.
- "Two services cannot break the loan limit with two different items": the solutions chapter says this is exactly what the test does **not** prove; the README calls it a documented race.
- "Both succeed and the second is ignored": the assertion requires one success, not two.

excerpts.quote: This proves the per-item checkout operation is guarded. It does not prove that two services atomically observe a borrower’s active-loan count when they check out different equipment.
borrower-limit checks across different equipment remain a documented race.

notes.title: Making before / equal / after deterministic
notes.body:
The goal: every run of the test must see exactly the same "now", so the three boundary cases (one before, exactly equal, one after) are exact. The testing chapter gives the setup: a tiny `FixedClock` record that implements `IClock`, set before the services are constructed, with expiry and due dates written relative to it.

This works because the services read time only through `IClock` (for example `(clock ?? new SystemClock()).UtcNow` in `ReserveAsync`).

Why the other setups fall short:
- "`DateTimeOffset.UtcNow` with a one-second margin": a margin can never test the *equal* case, and the real clock moves while the test runs. The chapter says to replace `UtcNow` with the fixed clock.
- "Resolve `SystemClock` from the production container": that is still the real clock, so nothing is fixed.

excerpts.quote: private sealed record FixedClock(DateTimeOffset UtcNow) : IClock;
Tests should set the clock before constructing services, then pass expiry or due dates relative to that fixed value. This makes before, equal, and after cases deterministic.
If a test uses `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow`, replace it with the fixed clock.

notes.title: Why a SQLite test must read back through a new context
notes.body:
The goal is to prove what is **stored**, not what a variable says. With the in-memory store, your local `equipment` is the stored object, so checking it is enough. With `SqliteEquipmentStore` it is not: `GetAsync` uses `AsNoTracking()` and builds a fresh object from the row. Your local variable was never written back. The only honest check is to open a new `BorrowBoxDbContext`, read the row, and assert its Status is Available.

Why the other checks fall short:
- "Assert the local variable's Status": the solutions chapter says against SQLite that proves nothing at all.
- "Assert only that the exception was thrown": it says nothing about the stored state.
- "Assert `ExecuteUpdateAsync` returned 1": that call is part of checkout, not reservation; and 1 would mean the row *was* changed.

excerpts.quote: `SqliteEquipmentStore.GetAsync` uses `AsNoTracking()` and maps a row to a fresh `EquipmentItem`.
Against SQLite that same assertion proves nothing at all — your local `equipment` was never persisted after the mutation. You must assert on a value read back through a new context.
var stored = await new SqliteEquipmentStore(readContext).GetAsync(equipment.Id, CancellationToken.None);

notes.title: Proving CancelAsync checks equipment first
notes.body:
The goal is about **order**: the service must check the equipment state before it changes the reservation. To see order, set up a mismatch: an Active reservation whose equipment is Available (not Reserved). If the check comes first, the call throws `equipment.not_reserved` and the reservation is still Active. If the transition came first, the reservation would already be Cancelled when the error appeared.

In the code, `CancelAsync` tests `equipment.Status != EquipmentStatus.Reserved` and throws before `reservation.Cancel()`.

Why the other observations fall short:
- "Cancelling twice returns the same reservation": the second cancel fails the Active check, and it says nothing about equipment.
- "Cancelled, equipment stays Available": that is the bug the goal wants to catch.
- "Throws `reservation.not_found`": the reservation exists; that code is for a missing id.

excerpts.quote: if (equipment.Status != EquipmentStatus.Reserved) throw new BorrowBoxException("equipment.not_reserved", "Equipment is not reserved for this reservation."); reservation.Cancel();
An active reservation paired with Available equipment should throw `equipment.not_reserved` before `reservation.Status` changes.
